To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the location of the sudden decrease in lithium abundance for subgiants with masses higher than about 1 M is the same as that of the discontinuies in rotation and Ca II emission flux.

(1) the location of the decrease in rotation, CaII emission flux (and, to a lesser extent, lithium) is a function of mass, and (2) the decrease in rotation occurs earlier than that in CaII emission flux.
the discontinuities observed in the rotation, chromospheres, and lithium abundance are related to the mass of stars.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the behavior of the rotation and chromospheric activity in relation to stellar evolution.
the link between rotation and chromospheric activity, and between rotation and lithium abundance, in the case of subgiant stars.
a link between rotation, CaII emission and lithium abundance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lithium abundance of subgiants is related to their rotation rate and to their CaII emission flux but that this relation is not linear.

the rotation, CaII flux, and lithium abundance of subgiant stars are linked together, and that the location of the drop in these three parameters is determined by the mass of the star and the mass of its convective envelope.
the lithium abundance is a good indicator of stellar age for stars with masses below 1.2 Msolar and that it is not so for higher masses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the location of the sudden decrease in rotation and Ca II emission flux for subgiant stars is related to the increase in mass of the convectively mixed region, whereas the decrease in lithium content is related to the decrease in the mass of lithium-rich layers.
rotation and CaII are more closely related than rotation and lithium.
the location of the drop in lithium abundance is determined by the mass of the star and that the location of rotation and Ca II emission is determined by the depth of the convective zone.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the location of the sudden decrease in the rotation, CaII emission fluxes, and lithium abundance for stars with masses between 1.2 and 1.5 M are in the same region, around the F8IV spectral type, and are related to the deepening of their convective envelopes.
the discontinuities observed in the behavior of rotation, CaII emission fluxes and lithium abundance in subgiants are not due to the same physical mechanism.
there is no simple correlation between rotation, CaII flux, and lithium abundance in the sample of subgiants.
